title: What Happens to Truth?
hook: When anything can be faked and the internet floods with synthetic everything, the danger isn't just believing lies — it's the 'liar's dividend,' where real evidence gets dismissed as fake too.
key_points: Cheap, convincing fakes erode the default trust we place in photos, audio, and video.
The 'liar's dividend': real wrongdoing can be waved away as 'probably AI'.
A flood of synthetic content makes finding reliable signal harder, not just riskier.
Trust shifts from the artifact to the source — provenance becomes everything.
content_html: The deepest question AI raises for everyday life isn't about any single fake — it's what happens to truth itself when fakery becomes cheap, convincing, and endless. For a century, a photograph or a recording carried a kind of automatic credibility: seeing was believing. AI is dissolving that default. Once people internalize that any image, voice, or video might be synthetic, the comfortable shortcut of trusting our eyes stops working, and every piece of evidence carries a question mark.
extra_html: The first-order worry — people believing convincing lies — is real but almost obvious. The subtler and more corrosive effect is the "liar's dividend." When everyone knows realistic fakes exist, the genuinely guilty gain a powerful escape hatch: caught on tape, they can simply claim the tape is AI. Real evidence of real wrongdoing can be shrugged off as "probably fake," and doubt becomes a weapon. Layer on the sheer volume — a flood of synthetic articles, images, reviews, and comments — and the problem isn't only that lies spread; it's that reliable signal gets buried in noise, and a tired public retreats into either gullibility or blanket cynicism. Neither is healthy for a society that has to make decisions together. There's no tidy fix, but the direction is clear: trust has to migrate from the artifact to the source. Provenance — who is vouching for this, what's their track record, is it independently confirmed — becomes the thing that matters, and technologies to certify where content came from are part of the response. For individuals, the takeaway is a mindset: hold your beliefs about online media a little more loosely, anchor to sources you've earned reason to trust, and resist the lazy slide into believing everything or nothing.

related.title: Deepfakes & Misinformation
related.hook: Seeing is no longer believing. AI can now fake a photo, a voice, or a video convincingly enough to fool a quick glance — so the new skill is knowing when to doubt.

related.title: Spotting AI-Made Content
related.hook: There are real tells for AI text and images — but they're fading fast, and 'AI detector' tools are unreliable. The durable skill is judging the source, not squinting at the pixels.

related.title: AI & the News
related.hook: AI now writes news, fakes whole 'outlets,' and powers the feed deciding what you see. Staying informed increasingly means knowing how the sausage is made — and who made it.

flashcards.explanation_html: Once everyone knows convincing fakes exist, the guilty can dismiss genuine audio or video of themselves as 'just AI' — doubt itself becomes a shield.

flashcards.prompt: As fakes get better, where does trust have to move?
flashcards.back_html: From the artifact to the source — we increasingly judge a photo or claim by who provides it and whether it's confirmed, not by how real it looks.
